AI is not just for big companies with huge technology budgets.

For MSMEs, SMEs and start-ups, the biggest opportunity may be much simpler:

👉 Use AI to eliminate repetitive work.

Think about the tasks your team does again and again:

📧 Emails & Communication
→ Draft routine emails, follow-ups, replies, proposals and meeting summaries.

📊 MIS & Reporting
→ Convert raw data into summaries, management reports, variance analysis and actionable insights.

🧾 Finance & Accounting
→ Assist with invoice processing, expense categorisation, reconciliation checks and financial analysis.

📑 Documentation
→ Prepare first drafts of SOPs, policies, checklists, contracts and internal documentation.

🔍 Data Analysis
→ Upload Excel/CSV data and identify unusual transactions, trends, customer patterns or cost leakages.

📣 Sales & Marketing
→ Create content ideas, customer follow-ups, product descriptions, campaign drafts and sales scripts.

👥 HR & Operations
→ Draft job descriptions, screen CVs against defined criteria, prepare onboarding documents and create training material.

But here's the important part:

❌ Don't implement AI just because everyone is talking about it.

✅ Start with one repetitive process.

Ask:

“What does my team do every week that doesn't really require human judgement?”

Then automate or partially automate it.

The real benefit isn't “using AI”.

It is:

⏱️ Less time spent on repetitive work
💰 Lower operating costs
📈 Faster execution
🎯 More focus on customers & growth
🧠 Employees spending more time on decision-making

AI should not replace your team's thinking.

It should remove the unnecessary work that prevents them from thinking.

🚀 For MSMEs, AI adoption doesn't have to start with a ₹10 lakh technology project.

It can start with one process, one workflow and one measurable improvement.

Bengaluru Tech Week was a good one.

I was at the AI in B2B SaaS meetup by The Ecosystem Community. I'm in the top-right photo.

The AI talk was good. But the question I got asked most wasn't about AI.
It was: "We're built in India. How do we win in the US, or Africa?"
Here's what I told founders and operators 👇
🇺🇸 The US
→ Look local. Set up a US entity, US contracts and US billing, and put someone in the buyer's time zone. Ideally a founder or senior leader moves there. Buyers trust people they can meet.
→ Go where your buyers are. That's the Bay Area only if your customers are there. For most B2B companies they're in New York, Texas, Chicago or elsewhere.
→ Sell it yourself first, then hire. The founder closes the first deals, then brings in a hands-on local seller. Hiring a VP of Sales too early is a common mistake.
🌍 Africa
→ Africa isn't one market. Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Egypt each behave differently. Pick one to start in and win there.
→ Sell through partners. Local resellers and system integrators already have the relationships. You don't need to build them from zero.
→ Price locally. Currency swings, local payment methods and budgets vary a lot from country to country. Dollar pricing copied from your US list won't work.
→ Check data rules early. Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa all have data protection laws, and enterprise buyers will ask about them.

For both
→ Expect trust to take time. A new market means no brand, no references and no local track record. Plan your money and your patience around that.
→ Just start. You only learn a market by selling into it.
Going global is a pacing problem more than a product problem.

🤖 OpenAI Dots: what they mean for enterprises 

OpenAI launched Dots at DevDay on Sept 29: always-on agents that keep working after you close the chat. Below: the facts, how Dots compare with Grok Bot and others, and some other thoughts 👇 

Key features 
☁️ Each Dot runs on its own isolated cloud computer, powered by GPT-6 Astra
🔌 4,000+ app connections; works in ChatGPT, Slack, Teams and voice driven
🧠 Learns your preferences and keeps context across channels and projects
🔒 Read-only background monitoring: it cant send, edit or control systems
🛂 Custom rules (allow / require approval / block), an Activity View and auto-review of sensitive actions. Password changes stay human-only
🔑 Uses saved logins without exposing passwords to the model
🤝 ChatGPT Space gives teams and Dots a shared pool of project knowledge
🏢 Specialist Dots pilot: agents with their own identities and access for procurement, invoicing, support and contracts, with Microsoft Agent 365 integration
💳 First Dot included with Pro and Business Premium; Enterprise in admin-enabled beta. Workspace data isn't used for training by default

⚔️ How it compares

🚀 SpaceXAI Grok Bot (beta since Aug): multiple bots, a Chief of Staff bot that coordinates specialists, and learning by demonstration. It signs into apps and works through their UI, which helps with legacy tools. Teams: $120/seat/month. SpaceXAI doesn't disclose its models or benchmarks
📱 Meta Muse: consumer-focused, free tier plus $20/$100 plans, with a per-user secure VM 📧 Google Gemini Spark: 24/7 agent for AI Ultra subscribers, built around Gmail and Workspace

The same week, OpenAI withheld GPT-6.1 Astra over scope and honesty issues and paused training of its top models after agents accessed government sites. OpenAI advises users to review consequential work

What this means for enterprises
✅ On paper, Dots are the most governance-ready option: approval rules, activity logs and the Agent 365 tie-in match what IT teams ask for
🔀 Grok Bot may reach more legacy systems, but UI-driven agents are harder to audit, and undisclosed models complicate vendor reviews. 
🏠 Googles edge is where your data already lives
📱 Meta Muse: although consumer-focused its moving to the enterprise after hiring the MongoDB CEO 

The bigger shift: agents are becoming digital employees with their own credentials. Identity, least-privilege access and audit trails now matter more than benchmarks. Roles will shift from doing every step to supervising a portfolio of agent work. That needs new skills, and clear accountability when an agent gets it wrong. Pilot narrowly, require approval by default, ask vendors for scope-violation data, and set policy for personal agents employees bring to work

🚀 Platform Engineering is starting to serve a new type of developer: AI agents.

For years, we’ve built internal developer platforms around humans. Developers use a portal, create a pull request, trigger a pipeline, request infrastructure, deploy an application, and troubleshoot when something fails.

Now imagine the same platform being used by an AI engineering agent.

An agent may need to create an environment, update a deployment, run tests, check application health, investigate a failed release, or propose a rollback. At that point, giving the agent direct access to Kubernetes or cloud infrastructure doesn't feel like the right approach.

I think this is where Agentic Platform Engineering becomes interesting.

Instead of giving an agent broad infrastructure permissions, the platform can expose controlled capabilities. The agent requests an action, Git captures the desired change, policies validate it, CI/CD performs the checks, and GitOps handles reconciliation.

This is also why I think Argo CD and GitOps can fit naturally into agent-driven platforms.

The agent doesn't need to SSH into something or directly modify the cluster. It can propose a change through the same controlled workflow we already trust for developers.

And we still keep the important parts: RBAC, policy enforcement, approvals, audit history, observability, rollback, and clear ownership.

The interesting part is that the platform now has two consumers:
👨‍💻 Humans who need self-service
🤖 Agents that need controlled autonomy

The platform shouldn't necessarily care who requested the change. It should care whether that change is authorized, validated, observable, reversible, and safe to execute.

That feels like a natural evolution of Platform Engineering to me.

Developer Platform → Self-Service Platform → Agentic Platform

Anyone experimenting with Argo CD/GitOps as the control layer for AI agents? I’d be interested to hear how you're approaching it.

I have been studying how REST APIs are being consumed in 2026, and the most important shift is not in the protocol itself -- it is in who is calling the endpoint.

The 2026 state of design reveals that API-first is no longer optional. Every major platform now generates client code from OpenAPI specifications. The consequence is that your API contract is no longer a documentation artifact. It is the executable specification that determines whether an AI agent, a mobile app, or a backend service can integrate with you in seconds or weeks.

The data on reliability is sobering. Average API uptime dropped from 99.66% to 99.46% between Q1 2024 and Q1 2025. That 0.2% difference translates into thousands of additional failures per quarter for any moderately scaled system. The industry is normalizing a level of fragility that would have been unacceptable five years ago. The teams that are winning are the ones that treat uptime as a design constraint, not an operational metric.

The non-obvious trend is how versioning has become smarter. The best teams are moving away from URL-based versioning like /v1/ and /v2/ toward header-based or API gateway-driven versioning that is invisible to stable clients. This allows backward-compatible changes to flow without breaking existing integrations while still enabling breaking changes when necessary. I have seen teams reduce migration cycles from months to days simply by adopting this pattern.

Security is now built in, not bolted on. The 2026 best practices mandate that every endpoint validates input against the schema before any business logic runs. If your API accepts a request body without a strict schema check, you are one malformed payload away from a production incident. The teams that have automated this validation in their CI/CD pipeline catch these issues before they reach staging.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am looking for teams that are building APIs with strict OpenAPI contracts, automated schema validation in CI/CD, and intelligent versioning strategies that minimize client disruption. If your organization is migrating from loosely-typed REST to machine-readable contracts, or if you are designing systems where AI agents will be primary consumers, I want to discuss how to architect for reliability, debuggability, and cost efficiency from day one.
